title: Moisture control & aspiration
blurb: High- and low-volume suction, rubber dam, cotton wool rolls and dry guards: keeping the field dry, clear and safe.
question: The hygienist is using an ultrasonic scaler on a patient with heavy deposits, and the mirror keeps misting over with spray and blood. Later the same day, the dentist asks for rubber dam before a composite. What should you do about the poor view, and what is rubber dam for?

teach.body: The mouth is wet, warm and full of saliva, and handpieces and scalers add a lot of water spray. Moisture control keeps the working area dry and visible. It matters for five reasons: the dentist can see; bonded materials such as composite fail if saliva touches them; the patient's airway is protected from water, debris and small instruments; the patient stays comfortable instead of choking on pooled water; and less contaminated aerosol escapes into the room.

teach.caption: Use the HVA whenever a handpiece, scaler or 3-in-1 spray is running. The saliva ejector cannot cope with spray or aerosol. Ask patients not to close their lips around it, which can draw fluid back from the line.

teach.h: Good aspiration: tip placement is everything
teach.body: Hold the HVA tip close to the tooth being treated, usually just distal to it and on the opposite side from where the dentist is working, with the opening parallel to the tooth surface. Keep it out of the dentist's line of sight and away from the soft palate, which triggers gagging. If the view becomes misty or blood pools, the fix is almost always to reposition the suction. Poor suction position means poor visibility.

teach.h: Three ways to keep the tooth dry
teach.caption: All three work alongside the high-volume aspirator, not instead of it. Wet a dry cotton roll or dry guard before removing it so the lining of the mouth isn't torn.

Rubber dam is essential for root canal treatment and strongly preferred for bonding. Check the medical history first: use non-latex dam for a latex allergy.

teach.h: Cotton wool rolls and dry guards
teach.body: Cotton wool rolls are quick and simple. They work best placed over the openings of the salivary ducts: in the buccal sulcus opposite the upper second molar for the parotid duct, and in the floor of the mouth beside the tongue for the submandibular ducts. Dry guards (absorbent triangular pads) sit on the inside of the cheek over the parotid duct. If a roll dries and sticks to the mucosa, wet it before removing it so the lining isn't torn.

teach.text: Don't confuse the two suction types. A saliva ejector only drains pooled saliva; it can't clear handpiece spray, blood or aerosol. That job needs the high-volume aspirator, held by you, right next to the tooth.

items: Aims: visibility, dry bonding, airway protection, comfort, less aerosol.
HVA: wide bore, nurse-held, close to the tooth, removes spray, debris, blood and aerosol.
Saliva ejector: narrow, low volume, removes pooled saliva only.
Rubber dam: isolation, moisture control, retraction, airway protection, asepsis. Tie floss to the clamp.
Cotton rolls over the duct openings; wet before removing. Misty view = reposition the HVA.

summary: You can now choose between high- and low-volume suction, position the HVA tip for a clear view, name every item in the rubber dam kit and what dam achieves, and use cotton rolls and dry guards correctly over the salivary duct openings.

A.q: Which item would you select to remove pooled saliva steadily during a restoration?
options: High-volume aspirator tip
3-in-1 syringe tip
Saliva ejector
Surgical aspirator tip
A.why: A saliva ejector is a narrow, low-volume tip that sits in the floor of the mouth and drains pooled saliva.

whyNot.0: The HVA is for spray, debris, blood and aerosol, held by the nurse.
whyNot.1: The 3-in-1 syringe delivers air and water; it doesn't remove fluid.
whyNot.3: A surgical aspirator is a fine tip for blood in surgical sites.

A.q: During root surface debridement, the operator's view becomes poor because of mist and spray. What is the best action?
options: Turn off the scaler water supply
Reposition the high-volume suction
Ask the patient to swallow more often
Add a second saliva ejector
A.why: A misty, flooded field is usually caused by poor HVA position. Moving the tip close to the working site restores visibility.

whyNot.0: The ultrasonic scaler needs water to cool the tip; turning it off is unsafe.
whyNot.2: Swallowing doesn't clear aerosol, and patients can't swallow safely mid-procedure.
whyNot.3: A saliva ejector can't cope with spray or aerosol.

A.q: Which statement best describes the purposes of rubber dam?
options: It numbs the tooth and reduces pain
It isolates the tooth and guards the airway
It whitens the tooth during treatment
It holds the matrix band firmly in position
A.why: Rubber dam isolates the tooth, keeps it dry, retracts soft tissues, protects the airway and improves asepsis.

whyNot.0: Local anaesthetic numbs the tooth; rubber dam doesn't.
whyNot.2: Rubber dam has no whitening effect.
whyNot.3: A matrix retainer and wedge hold the band; the dam isolates the tooth.

B.q: Why is a length of floss tied to the rubber dam clamp before placement?
options: To measure the tooth to choose the clamp size
To help stretch the dam sheet tighter
To retrieve the clamp if it slips or breaks
To clean between the teeth afterwards
B.why: The floss ligature lets the clamp be pulled out quickly if it comes loose, so it can't be swallowed or inhaled.

whyNot.0: Clamps are chosen by tooth type, not measured with floss.
whyNot.1: The frame keeps the sheet taut; the ligature is a safety line.
whyNot.3: Separate floss is used to ease the dam through contacts; the ligature is for safety.

B.q: The dentist wants an upper molar kept dry with cotton wool rolls. Where should the roll go?
options: In the buccal sulcus by the upper second molar
Under the tongue in the floor of the mouth
Against the hard palate behind the incisors
Between the lower lip and the lower incisor teeth
B.why: The parotid duct opens in the cheek opposite the upper second molar, so a roll in the upper buccal sulcus there soaks up its saliva.

whyNot.1: The floor of the mouth is where the submandibular ducts open, useful for lower teeth.
whyNot.2: There are no major duct openings on the hard palate behind the incisors.
whyNot.3: This would help lower anterior teeth, not an upper molar.

B.q: The dentist asks you to prepare a rubber dam sheet for a lower molar. Which instrument makes the hole in the sheet?
options: Clamp forceps
Rubber dam punch
Rubber dam frame
Matrix retainer
B.why: The rubber dam punch cuts clean holes of the right size in the sheet for the teeth.

whyNot.0: Clamp forceps open and place the clamp.
whyNot.2: The frame holds the sheet taut outside the mouth.
whyNot.3: A matrix retainer holds a matrix band; it isn't part of the dam kit.

C.q: The dentist starts cutting a cavity with the high-speed handpiece, which produces heavy water spray. Which suction should you use?
options: Saliva ejector on its own
A cotton wool roll
A dry guard pad
High-volume aspirator
C.why: Only the high-volume aspirator removes the volume of water spray and aerosol produced by a high-speed handpiece.

whyNot.0: A saliva ejector is low volume and would be overwhelmed.
whyNot.1: Cotton wool rolls absorb saliva at the duct openings; they can't remove spray.
whyNot.2: A dry guard absorbs saliva from the parotid duct, not handpiece spray.

C.q: A patient with a latex allergy needs rubber dam for root canal treatment. What should be used?
options: Cotton wool rolls instead, always
A non-latex rubber dam sheet
A standard dam with extra gloves
No isolation at all for this patient
C.why: Non-latex dam gives the same isolation and airway protection without exposing the patient to latex.

whyNot.0: Cotton rolls don't give the isolation or airway protection root canal treatment needs.
whyNot.2: Gloves don't protect the patient's face and mouth from a latex sheet.
whyNot.3: Root canal treatment should be done under rubber dam; leaving it off is unsafe.

C.q: At the end of a restoration, a cotton wool roll has dried and is stuck to the patient's cheek. What should you do?
options: Pull it away quickly in one movement
Leave it for the patient to remove later
Moisten it with water before removing it
Use the HVA to suck it off the cheek
C.why: Wetting the roll first loosens it, so the delicate lining of the cheek isn't torn when it comes away.

whyNot.0: Pulling a dry roll off can strip the mucosa and leave a painful ulcer.
whyNot.1: Leaving it in risks choking or the patient pulling it off and causing trauma.
whyNot.3: Sucking at a stuck roll may bruise the cheek and can pull the cotton into the suction.

reteach.title: Think of decorating a bathroom
reteach.question: You can't paint or grout a wet wall. How is restoring a tooth in a wet mouth like decorating a steamy bathroom?

blocks.h: Keep the wall dry, and keep the water out
blocks.body: A decorator opens a window and wipes down the wall before painting, because paint won't stick to a wet surface. Composite is the same: one touch of saliva and the bond fails. The HVA is your extractor fan, pulling away spray and steam where it's made. Cotton rolls are towels at the leaks (the salivary ducts). Rubber dam is a dust sheet with a hole cut out: only the tooth you are working on is exposed, and everything else, including the airway, is covered.

explain.body: A wide-bore tip held by the nurse close to the working tooth, opening parallel to the tooth surface, out of the dentist's view and away from the soft palate. It removes spray, debris, blood and aerosol and can retract the cheek or tongue.

test.q: Why should the HVA tip be kept away from the soft palate?
options: It can trigger the gag reflex
It reduces the suction power
It damages the suction tubing
It makes the tip harder to clean
test.why: Touching the soft palate or back of the tongue easily triggers gagging, which is unpleasant and unsafe mid-procedure.

whyNot.1: Suction power isn't affected by the palate.
whyNot.2: Tubing isn't damaged by tip position.
whyNot.3: Cleaning is the same wherever the tip has been.

explain.body: Sheet, punch, clamp, clamp forceps, frame and floss. It gives a dry field, airway protection, soft tissue retraction and asepsis. Essential for root canal treatment. Use non-latex for a latex allergy. Report tears or leaks at once.

test.q: During treatment, the rubber dam tears near the clamp and saliva starts leaking in. What should you do?
options: Seal the tear with composite
Tell the dentist straight away
Add more cotton rolls on top
Carry on and mention it later
test.why: A leaking dam no longer isolates the tooth, so the dentist needs to know immediately to re-isolate.

whyNot.0: Composite isn't a repair for a dam; it would contaminate the field.
whyNot.2: Cotton rolls won't restore a proper seal.
whyNot.3: Continuing with a leaking dam risks contamination and failure.

explain.body: Place them over the duct openings: the parotid duct opposite the upper second molar, and the submandibular ducts in the floor of the mouth. Dry guards sit on the cheek over the parotid duct. Wet dried rolls before removing them.

head: Duct
Opens
rows: Floor of mouth, by the frenum

test.q: Where is a dry guard (absorbent pad) usually placed?
options: Under the tongue, by the frenum
On the hard palate
On the cheek over the parotid duct
Across the inside of the lower lip
test.why: Dry guards are stuck to the inside of the cheek over the parotid duct opening to soak up its saliva.

whyNot.0: Under the tongue is where cotton rolls catch submandibular saliva.
whyNot.1: No major salivary duct opens on the hard palate.
whyNot.3: Dry guards aren't used on the lower lip; they go over the parotid duct opening.
